title: A Note to the Self Who Was There
subtitle: A shared memory does not need a happy ending to be met with a little more kindness.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a kitchen table with separate notebooks, reflecting quietly after a shared meal.
imageConcept: A warm, natural-light scene of two friends at a lived-in kitchen table, each with a notebook and a cup, sharing the quiet without reading over the other’s shoulder.
body: Some memories arrive with a verdict already attached: I should have known better. I should have said something. I made that awkward. When another person was there, the story can feel even more fixed, as though the moment belongs to both of you in exactly the same way. But remembering is not the same as reaching a final ruling. One way to loosen the verdict is to write a short note to the version of yourself who lived through an ordinary shared moment—not to rewrite what happened, and not to insist that it was secretly good. The point is to bring a little more context to the person you were then.
Not a letter to the other person

This is different from an unsent letter, an apology draft, or a plan to repair a relationship. The page is addressed to you. The other person may matter to the memory, but they are not its audience and do not need to answer. Nor is the exercise a demand to forgive yourself, find a lesson, or turn discomfort into gratitude. Perhaps the memory is a conversation that faltered, a family gathering where you felt out of place, or a small decision you keep replaying. You can acknowledge that it felt difficult without making the event more painful—or more uplifting—than you remember it.
What one study suggests—and what it cannot

A 2024 study in Frontiers in Psychology examined compassionate writing directed toward past and future selves. In one experiment, 150 undergraduates wrote letters to themselves; in another, 31 wrote about a past experience alone and 31 about one shared with someone. The researchers reported that focusing on a shared experience was more helpful for mood in that sample. That finding offers a reason to explore the idea, not a guarantee: the participants were healthy undergraduates in Japan, and the study does not show that this reflection works for everyone or for every memory [1].
Kindness should not become a promise

Evidence on writing exercises is mixed, and the difference between a carefully designed program and a single prompt matters. In a randomized online study of 425 German adults, one 15-minute self-compassion writing task did not significantly increase immediate self-compassion or positive affect compared with the control task. The authors suggested that the exercise may have been too brief or insufficiently specific [2]. In a separate randomized study, 68 undergraduates with high shame completed a 16-day letter-writing intervention or joined a waitlist; the intervention group showed reductions in shame, self-criticism, and general anxiety, maintained at one-month follow-up. That narrow sample and multi-day protocol do not establish that one short note treats anxiety or shame [3]. Taken together, these studies argue for modest expectations, not a promised mood lift.
Choose a memory with room around it

If you want to try this, choose something relatively ordinary and finished: a moment from a meal, a trip, a project, or a conversation with someone you know. Avoid beginning with the most painful event in your life. The aim is not to minimize what happened; it is to set a boundary that makes the reflection manageable. You might choose a memory that still carries a little self-criticism but does not feel overwhelming to approach today. If nothing comes to mind that feels safe enough, there is no need to force a choice. Skipping the exercise is a valid decision.
Write what you remember, not a transcript

Start with a few plain sentences about the scene: where you were, who else was there, and what you recall happening. Memory is partial, and people who shared an event may remember different details. You are not producing a record for anyone else to approve. If you are unsure, say so: “I remember feeling quiet; I don’t know what the others thought.” Then turn toward your past self as a supportive friend might. What were you carrying that day? What could you not have known yet? What pressure, hope, or limitation might have shaped your response? These questions add context without pretending that every choice was ideal.

The most useful line may be modest. “You were trying to get through a complicated evening” can feel more honest than “You did everything perfectly.” “You didn’t know how that conversation would unfold” leaves room for regret without making you responsible for predicting the future. You might also acknowledge the other people in the scene: they had their own perspectives, information, and needs, which you could not fully see. This is not a way to excuse harm or settle a disagreement. If someone was hurt, accountability and repair may still matter. The note simply lets you look at your own part with more than one lens.
A private page, or an optional shared moment

Give yourself a loose limit—perhaps ten minutes—and stop when you choose. Close the notebook when you have written one kind, believable sentence; you do not have to reach a conclusion. This practice can bring discomfort, and the 2024 study reported varied mood responses, including some participants whose mood became more negative. If the memory feels worse as you write, pause, put the page away, and return your attention to the present room. This is not a substitute for professional support. If you try it alongside a friend, each person should write privately and share only a sentence they freely choose to share; that paired format is an optional adaptation, not an outcome tested by the studies.
Leave the shared scene in its own hands

For a first try, pick one low-stakes memory you shared with someone: a meal that went quiet, a plan that changed, or a conversation you have replayed more than once. Set a ten-minute limit and write only what you remember, including what you do not know about the other person’s experience. Then address your past self with one sentence that feels kind and true, not flattering or absolving. Close the notebook. If you are doing this with someone else, keep the pages separate and let each person decide whether to share anything. The memory can remain complicated; the practice is simply to meet the person you were there with a little more context.
